strengths: The paper targets a genuinely relevant problem: designing a lightweight, modality-agnostic fusion frontend that is robust to missing modalities and does not entangle with feature-extractor gradients. The motivating analysis (Section 1, Appendix A) of four 'incomplete assumptions' in prior fusion work is thoughtful.

The proposed GMF is extremely simple (a few linear mapping matrices plus a reconstruction loss), and the reported parameter/FLOP counts (5.25M / 0.01G on VGGSound, 0.32M on ActivityNet) are dramatically lower than competitors, making the efficiency claim credible.

The appendix contains a substantial amount of supporting work: gradient-flow analysis, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 experiments on optimal feature dimensionality, ImageNet experiments on up-then-down linear projection, and a broad comparison table over fusion methods across task types (NMT/EMT/GMT), which shows real effort at empirical grounding.
The authors are candid in places: footnote 5 admits the PNP proof is incomplete, and the limitations of linear-layer parameter scaling are acknowledged in the conclusion.
weaknesses: The central 'theory' is largely metaphorical rather than rigorous. Treating features as charged particles governed by the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equation is an analogy; the final method is simply a linear up-projection, a fixed-index split into 'invariant'/'specific' halves, a cross-modal swap, and an MSE reconstruction loss. Nothing in the PNP derivation actually predicts or constrains this architecture, so the physical framing adds no falsifiable content. The claim of 'an exhaustive proof' (contribution 1) is directly contradicted by the authors' own footnote 5 ('The proof here is incomplete... we will provide full proof later').

The information-entropy formalism is loose. Conditional entropies H(Y|C(...)) are written over deterministic maps without measure-theoretic care, Eq. (4) applies a joint-entropy identity to f(X,θ) with an undefined 'mutual information' term, and Theorems 3.2/3.3 assert existence claims (e.g., an optimal integer dimension l_best) that are only supported by showing empirical accuracy curves, not proven. Theorem 3.3's probabilistic argument in Appendix D (Eq. 41-44) treats gradient updates as continuous random variables in a way that does not constitute a proof.

Experimental support for the headline claims is weak. On VGGSound, GMF does not achieve SOTA (32.01 AV vs. 33.77 for MISA and 33.23 for DrFuse); the claim of surpassing SOTA holds only for the combined G-Perceiver/G-MBT variants or the GMF-MAE configuration, which uses a much stronger feature extractor (MAE/Audio-MAE) than all baselines, making that comparison unfair.

Experimental rigor is thin: all results use a single fixed random seed ('1') with no variance or significance testing, despite many reported gaps of well under one point; several FakeAVCeleb methods (including the baseline and GMF itself) report identical ACC of 97.68, suggesting majority-class degenerate solutions that are not analyzed; and the FakeAVCeleb split is a custom 70/30 per-class split rather than the community standard.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is released, and the appendix itself states that 'the reported experimental results may not be fully reproducible.' The GMF-MAE variant (which produces the paper's best results) explicitly has 'open source code... not yet available.'

Presentation quality hampers assessment: notation is dense and inconsistent (Zi vs Ẑ vs P matrices with j and j+1 indices), key quantities like the dissociation boundary b(j) are set by heuristic (always half the dimension), Figures 2 and 7 are hard to parse, and an unexplained footnote 'Changes have been made here from the original' appears in the methodology. The narrative frequently mixes conjecture and theorem in ways that make the actual contribution (a linear swap-and-reconstruct fusion layer) hard to separate from the physics narrative.

The claim that reducing mutual information between features 'lowers the entropy of downstream tasks' and thereby improves performance is asserted theoretically but never verified empirically — no experiment measures the entropy/mutual-information quantities the theory centers on, so the mechanism connecting PNP theory to the observed gains remains untested.

strengths: The proposed GMF module is extremely lightweight (four linear mappings per modality), and the paper reports favorable parameter/FLOP trade-offs (e.g., 5.25M params, 0.01G FLOPs on VGGSound), which is a practically relevant angle.

The evaluation spans three different task types (retrieval on ActivityNet, event classification on VGGSound, deepfake detection on FakeAVCeleb) and includes a frozen-vs-trainable extractor protocol that probes the fusion module somewhat independently of the extractors, which is a reasonable experimental design idea.

The paper attempts to connect fusion design to a theoretical objective (entropy-based conditioning on downstream tasks), and the motivation that fully aligning modalities can harm downstream task-specific information is a legitimate and interesting observation.

The appendix contains a fair amount of supporting material (gradient flow discussion, dimension-mapping experiments on CIFAR/ImageNet, algorithmic pseudocode), showing effort at transparency about the method's actual implementation.
weaknesses: The physical theory is an analogy, not a derivation. Mapping feature vectors onto charged particles in a 1D electrolytic cell rests on many unjustified assumptions (constant excitation field, negligible advection, 'features from another modality are perfectly ordered', etc.), and the authors themselves footnote that the key proof is 'incomplete... we will provide full proof later.' This directly contradicts the claimed 'exhaustive proof' in the contributions.

Theorems 3.1–3.3 are either restatements of known phenomena (optimal representation dimensionality, cf. double descent [42]) or not rigorously proven. The 'proof' of Theorem 3.3 mixes a rank argument with an informal probability argument (Eqs. 41–44) that assumes gradient adjustments follow a continuous distribution without justification. Conjecture 3.1 is explicitly a conjecture, yet Figure 12 presents hypothetical curves as if they substantiate the method.

The actual method is essentially: linear up-projection, a fixed index-based split of features into two segments (boundary fixed at half the dimension), cross-modal concatenation of one segment each, and an MSE reconstruction loss. The PNP framework contributes nothing identifiable to the architecture or loss. Missing ablations (e.g., random split, no split, no reconstruction loss, varying n and b) leave it unclear whether the mechanism matters at all versus a trivial learned linear reparameterization close to MISA-style shared/specific decomposition.

Experimental rigor is weak: a single fixed random seed ('1'), single runs with no variance or significance testing, very low absolute accuracies on VGGSound (~28–35%) where differences of 1–2 points are treated as meaningful, and non-standard, self-defined data splits (70/30 split for FakeAVCeleb; 20% of VGGSound samples dropped).

The headline 'surpass SOTA' result (GMF-MAE, 99.99/99.97) uses substantially stronger feature extractors (MAE, Audio-MAE) than all compared methods, making the comparison unfair; several baselines in Table 4 tie exactly at 97.68 ACC, suggesting possible evaluation artifacts. GMF alone does not outperform SOTA in the main comparisons.

Notation is inconsistent and confusing throughout (U vs. P matrices between Theorem 3.4 and Eq. 15-17; P_spec vs. P_cspec in Eq. 17; a stray footnote 'Changes have been made here from the original'), and the writing contains numerous grammatical errors that impede comprehension of an already dense theory section.
No code is released (footnote states the open-source implementation is 'not yet available'), and combined with the nonstandard splits and single-seed protocol, reproducibility is poor.

The central empirical claim — that entropy reduction via dissociation is the operative mechanism — is never measured (no mutual information or entropy estimates are reported), so the theory and the experiments remain disconnected.

strengths: The core empirical contribution is potentially useful: GMF is an extremely lightweight (linear-only) fusion frontend that performs competitively with much heavier fusion modules (e.g., G-MBT, G-Perceiver) while using far fewer parameters (5.25M, 0.01G FLOPs on VGGSound), and it shows noticeably better robustness to missing modalities (e.g., A-only 21.55 vs. much larger drops for MBT/AVoiD-DF baselines), which is a practically valuable property.

The paper attempts a principled framing: it explicitly defines optimization objectives via conditional entropy (Eqs. 1-5), motivates why full modality alignment can hurt downstream tasks, and designs experiments around three controlled settings (frozen extractor, trainable extractor, method-specific extractors), which is a thoughtful evaluation design.

The taxonomy of NMT/EMT/GMT tasks and Table 1's systematic comparison of prior fusion methods (alignment, gradient coupling, missing-modality handling, complexity) is a useful organizational contribution.

The paper is reasonably transparent about weaknesses in several places: it acknowledges incomplete proofs (footnote 5), non-reproducibility caveats from dropout seeding, admits that MISA/DrFuse outperform GMF on VGGSound, and discusses linear-layer parameter growth as a limitation.
Reproducibility details are extensive: hyperparameters, preprocessing, seeds, and algorithmic pseudocode (Appendix J) are provided for the main GMF method.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim—the mapping of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equation onto feature fusion—is not rigorously established. The PNP-to-loss 'derivation' (Appendix B) is an analogy, not a proof: physical quantities (charge, potential, temperature) are mapped to feature dimensions by assertion, and the paper itself concedes the proof is incomplete ('we will provide full proof later'). Nothing in the derivation actually constrains the final architecture, which is just four learnable linear matrices plus an MSE reconstruction loss; the same method could be described without any physics, suggesting the theory is decorative rather than load-bearing.

The theorems are not genuinely established results. Theorem 3.2 asserts existence of an optimal feature dimension but is supported only by CIFAR-10/100/ ImageNet empirical plots; Theorem 3.3 claims a strict inequality H(Y|f) < H(Y|U1·(U2·f)) but the 'proof' only gives a rank argument (≤) plus a loose probabilistic heuristic (Eqs. 41-44) that assumes gradient steps follow continuous distributions and hand-waves constants. Internal logic is also inconsistent: Eq. (4) states minimizing fused entropy ⇔ maximizing feature mutual information, while later sections argue downstream tasks require minimizing mutual information between modalities—the paper never reconciles this tension.

The claim that GMF 'identifies' modality-invariant vs. modality-specific features is weakly supported: the split is a positional slice of a learned linear expansion at b = l/2, with only a cross-modal reconstruction loss pushing toward invariance. There is no ablation, probe, or analysis verifying that the 'invariant' block actually captures modality-invariant information, so a central mechanistic claim is unverified.

Experimental rigor is insufficient for the claims. All results use a single fixed random seed ('1') with no variance or significance testing, yet several conclusions rest on small margins (e.g., GMF 31.64 vs. MISA 32.85 on VGGSound AV; ActivityNet mAP gaps of ~0.006-0.014). In Table 4, six methods tie at exactly 97.68 ACC, indicating a degenerate/saturated accuracy regime, and comparisons mix different feature extractors (MAE-based GMF-MAE vs. R(2+1)D baselines), making the 99.99/99.97 result an unfair attribution of gains to the fusion method rather than the extractor. The 'surpass SOTA' claim in the abstract is thus not well supported by controlled evidence.

GMF does not actually beat SOTA in the headline EMT comparison (Table 2): DrFuse and MISA exceed it in the complete-modality setting; the paper's contribution there reduces to 'comparable accuracy with fewer parameters plus missing-modality robustness,' which is more modest than the framing suggests.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: numerous grammatical errors ('an conjecture', 'GMF disassociated features which extracted by'), typos ('Reconsturction', 'Denote v̂', spurious superscripts '≈ 0⁴' in Eqs. 29/30), an editorial footnote ('Changes have been made here from the original') left in the manuscript, and notation inconsistencies (P vs. U for mapping matrices across Sections 3.4 and 4).

Reproducibility gaps remain: the GMF-MAE code is explicitly 'not yet available' (footnote 6), and that variant produces the paper's most striking results (Table 4/7); FakeAVCeleb uses a non-standard 70/30 class-sorted split rather than the official protocol, complicating comparison with prior work.

The claimed novelty over existing disentanglement approaches (Uni-Code, MISA, DrFuse) is unclear: GMF essentially performs linear expansion, a positional split into 'invariant'/'specific' blocks, cross-modal swap, and reconstruction—mechanically similar to shared-specific factorization methods—so the PNP framing, rather than a new mechanism, is the main differentiator.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (ActivityNet retrieval, FakeAVCeleb deepfake detection, CMU-MOSEI missing-modality sentiment) targeting three distinct failure modes (unequal-length inputs, modality conflict, missing modalities).

Thorough ablation studies (Tab. 8-11) covering each component (expansion, reconstruction loss, contrastive replacement, reconstruction metric, lambda, b, n), plus useful supplementary analyses in the appendix: runtime/memory profiling (Tab. 13), branch masking (Tab. 14), and multi-seed stability results (98.63±0.08 AUC), which strengthen reproducibility beyond the single fixed seed used in the main tables.

Gradient-level analysis (Fig. 4: cosine similarity of task vs. auxiliary gradients, gradient norm over training, t-SNE of shared/specific subspaces) directly probes the paper's central mechanism rather than only reporting end-task numbers, and the modality-order robustness test (Tab. 7) addresses an obvious concern with the cyclic design.
Clear articulation of the design motivation (fusion must act as both information coupler and gradient distributor) and an honest limitations discussion (quadratic cost of expansion).
weaknesses: The 'Self-Consistent Field' framing is largely metaphorical and over-sold. The PNP/SCF discussion (Sec. 3.2) provides intuition only, and the formalization in Eq. (1) is never enforced, verified, or theoretically connected to the method. The paper states 'see Appendix C for derivations,' but Appendix C is a general discussion of gradient flow and residual connections, not derivations of Eq. (1) - a notable claim-evidence mismatch.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing shared/specific disentanglement work (e.g., Wang et al. 2023a, MISA, DrFuse). The core recipe - expansion, shared/specific split, reconstruction loss - is standard; the cyclic shared-component substitution is the main new element, and its mechanistic justification (why substituting modality k's shared component into modality m helps) is asserted rather than analyzed. How missing modalities are handled by the cyclic path at inference time is never clearly described.

Baseline comparability is questionable: Tab. 4 mixes numbers reproduced by the authors (with different backbones per baseline, e.g., sLSTM for MISA, R(2+1)D-34 for DrFuse) with numbers copied from original papers for several methods, under an extremely imbalanced dataset (real:fake ~1:39). Comparing accuracy/AUC across heterogeneous feature extractors and sources weakens the headline gains on FakeAVCeleb.

Improvements on two of three benchmarks are marginal: ActivityNet mAP@10 improves 0.363 vs. 0.358 over AdaMMS, and CMU-MOSEI accuracy 87.8 vs. 87.6. Without statistical significance testing (only post-hoc multi-seed variance on two settings is given), these gains are within plausible noise, while the strong FakeAVCeleb gains carry the comparability concerns above.

The claimed mechanism ('task gradients must reach encoders cleanly') is supported qualitatively (Fig. 4 plots) but no quantitative, statistically controlled comparison of gradient statistics across methods is provided, and the extractor-degradation protocol in Tab. 6 uses bespoke baseline configurations described only loosely ('the network is consistent with SCFAE, but...').

Reproducibility is partial: code availability is described only in prose with no de-anonymized link, and key details of the missing-modality inference procedure and shared/specific boundary semantics are spread across the text, making independent reimplementation non-trivial.

strengths: The empirical protocol is unusually thorough for this area: ablations of the expansion mechanism, reconstruction loss vs. contrastive replacement, reconstruction metric (MSE vs. cosine), sensitivity to n, b, and λ, modality-order robustness (Tab. 7), branch masking (Tab. 14), runtime/memory profiling (Tab. 13), and multi-seed stability (App. B.3).

The diagnostic analysis in Tab. 6 (unimodal probing after joint training) and the gradient statistics in Fig. 4 (task/auxiliary gradient cosine, gradient norm trajectories) directly test the paper's central mechanism claim rather than only reporting end-task numbers.
The taxonomy in Tab. 1 (Align./Ref./Avail. axes) is a useful organizing lens for the fusion literature, and the related-work coverage is broad and current.

The design is lightweight (24M params, ~0.7ms forward on the studied configuration) and operates only at the fusion stage, which makes it easy to plug into existing pipelines with frozen or pre-trained encoders.
Writing and figures (e.g., Fig. 3 architecture diagram) are generally clear, and the limitation about quadratic parameter growth from expansion is stated honestly.
weaknesses: The headline 'Self-Consistent Field' framing is metaphorical rather than technical. Eq. (2) is a generic two-functional dynamical-system statement, and the method is never actually formulated as a field or analyzed via PNP dynamics. The physical analogy (drift/diffusion/self-consistency) decorates but does not generate the method: the actual mechanism is expand → split shared/specific → cyclically swap shared components → task + reconstruction loss, which is a fairly standard shared-specific disentanglement recipe (close in spirit to MISA, DLF, and shared-specific modeling of Wang et al. 2023a).

The formalization is a decoy. Eq. (1) poses a constrained bilevel-style objective that is neither solved, approximated, nor theoretically analyzed; the paper defers to 'Appendix C for derivations,' but Appendix C turns out to be generic background on backpropagation and residual connections with no derivation of Eq. (1) or proof that SCFAE satisfies the constraint.

A central claim — robustness to missing modalities — lacks a mechanical explanation. The cyclic substitution in Eq. (4) requires the shared component of another modality; the paper never states how the forward pass (or training) is adapted when a modality is absent at test time in Tab. 5. This gap makes the main missing-modality results hard to interpret or trust.

Baseline comparability is questionable. Appendix A.2 states that many baseline numbers are copied from original papers under possibly different feature extractors and splits, while SCFAE's are self-run. On CMU-MOSEI the paper asserts the feature setup 'is exactly the same as MCULoRA,' but this is asserted rather than demonstrated, and Tab. 5 mixes numbers of uncertain provenance. On FakeAVCeleb, Concat, MISA, DrFuse, Coupled Mamba, SALM, DLF, AdaMMS, and SCFAE all report the identical AV value 97.68, which suggests a shared protocol artifact and undermines fine-grained comparisons.

Improvements over the strongest recent baselines are small and within ranges the appendix seed study implies are near noise (e.g., ActivityNet mAP@10: 0.367 vs. 0.360 for AdaMMS; CMU-MOSEI avg: 87.8 vs. 87.6/87.4). The large margins claimed in the teaser (Fig. 1C) rest on the degradations of weaker baselines, not on separation from the state of the art.

The 'gradient conflict' narrative oversimplifies. Reconstruction is itself an auxiliary loss; the paper's own Fig. 4A shows it is merely near-orthogonal to the task gradient, and the contrastive-replacement ablation (Tab. 8) differs by ~0.03 mAP. The evidence supports 'reconstruction is a mild, compatible regularizer' more than the strong claim that prior decoupled methods are fundamentally broken by gradient interference.

Reproducibility is only partial: the code release covers only the authors' reproduction, with readers directed to third-party repositories for baselines, and no links are provided; the fixed-seed main results with seed-variance relegated to the appendix make headline numbers hard to audit.
Notation and citation hygiene issues (e.g., 'CMMP (Radford et al., 2021)' naming CLIP, 'As shown in 12', dangling references) suggest insufficient polish for a main-track submission.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely relevant problem—gradient flow from the task loss to modality encoders being distorted by fusion design—and grounds the evaluation in this framing rather than reporting accuracy alone.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: three distinct benchmarks (ActivityNet retrieval, FakeAVCeleb detection, CMU-MOSEI sentiment) chosen to test separate claimed challenges (unequal lengths, conflicting signals, missing modalities), plus structural ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity (n, b, λ), modality-order robustness, and a metric ablation for the reconstruction loss.

The gradient-level analysis (Fig. 4) directly probes the central claim: gradient-angle statistics between task and auxiliary gradients, task-gradient magnitude over training, and t-SNE of shared/specific subspaces, giving mechanistic evidence beyond end-task metrics.

Honest and useful limitation discussion (quadratic cost of expansion), and the appendix adds runtime/memory profiling, branch-masking ablations, and multi-seed stability (98.63±0.08 AUC; 0.3263±0.0023 mAP), which strengthens reproducibility confidence.
The proposed module is lightweight (~24M params, negligible latency overhead per Table 13) and leaves pretrained encoders untouched, which is a practical advantage.
weaknesses: The 'Self-Consistent Field' / Poisson–Nernst–Planck framing is largely decorative. The actual method is a shared/specific decomposition with cyclic exchange of shared components and a reconstruction loss; the drift/diffusion/unified-potential mapping is asserted rather than derived, and no property of SCF is used or validated. The formalization in Eq. (1) is also informal—the per-encoder argmin constraint is never analyzed or enforced.

The core mechanism has strong prior-art overlap: shared/specific factorization with cross-modal sharing is essentially the recipe of MISA, DrFuse, and particularly AVoiD-DF-style exchange of shared features, and the 'reconstruction preserves information' idea is standard. The claimed novelty relative to these is thin and the paper does not clearly articulate what is genuinely new beyond the particular cyclic substitution pattern.

The margins over the strongest baselines are modest: on CMU-MOSEI the gain over DLF/AdaMMS is ~0.2–0.4 ACC, and on ActivityNet ~0.007–0.01 mAP. With single-seed main results (multi-seed only in the appendix) and saturated accuracy on FakeAVCeleb (97.68 for several methods), the statistical significance of these gains is not established.

The most important claim—robustness to missing modalities—is not mechanistically explained. The cyclic self-consistent step requires all modalities' shared components at both train and inference; how inference proceeds when one or two modalities are absent (which projections are used, whether Z_shared is replaced, imputed, or masked) is never specified. This is a reproducibility gap for the headline result.

Baseline comparisons have fairness concerns: Table 4 mixes results taken from original papers under potentially different splits/encoders (acknowledged in A.2), some baselines appear weak relative to their published numbers, and the AV accuracy column is nearly identical across many methods, making the comparison ambiguous.

Several analyses are qualitative: Fig. 4's gradient-conflict histogram and bottleneck curves lack baselines' detailed statistics, and the claim that reconstruction loss 'mainly shapes the specific subspace' while task loss 'mainly shapes the shared subspace' is stated but never directly verified.
